fixes.explanation: Jesus did say that one, just somewhere else. It's in John 6:35, when He says, “I am the bread of life.” Here in chapter 9, though, He's talking about daytime and night, so the name that fits is the light of the world. Good catch on a real saying of His, just from a different chapter.
True, friend. Jesus tells him to go wash in the Pool of Siloam, and the man goes, washes and comes back seeing. Blind from birth when he leaves, seeing when he returns.
The text says otherwise, baker. Jesus tells him to go wash in the Pool of Siloam, and the man went and washed, and came back seeing. So he followed what Jesus told him, and he came back seeing.
Not quite, baker. The man never claims to be anybody's brother. The text says he kept saying, “I am the one.” He's the same man who used to sit and beg, and he says so.

That's right, friend. When they ask where Jesus is, he answers, “I do not know…” He can tell them everything about what happened to his eyes, but not where Jesus has gone. I like how plainly he says it.
The text doesn't call it a fasting day, friend. John 9:14 tells us it was a Sabbath. Nothing in the passage mentions fasting. Keep your eye on that Sabbath, because it matters in what comes next.
That's right, baker. He doesn't refuse. He tells the Pharisees, “He put mud on my eyes, and I washed, and now I can see.” He gives them an answer right there.

Good question, but nobody asks it here. These Pharisees ask, “How can a sinful man perform such signs?” Their question is about the signs, not about authority. And the text says there was division among them.

You got it, baker. Asked what he says about Jesus, since it was his eyes that were opened, the man replies, “He is a prophet…” Earlier he said, “The man they call Jesus,” and now he says prophet. I think that's a step up, and he says it out loud.
Yes, friend. They say, “…and we know he was born blind.” They stand behind that part plainly. It fits what the man himself says: “I was blind, but now I see!”
Not deaf, baker. The parents say he was born blind. Nothing in the passage says he was deaf. His eyes are the whole story here.
Not lame, friend. His parents say he was born blind. Nothing in the passage says he was lame. His eyes are what changed.

The text says the opposite, friend. His parents answer, “But how he can now see or who opened his eyes, we do not know.” The text says they said this because they were afraid of the Jews. So they hand the rest back with, “Ask him.”

That's it, baker. The text says, “His parents said this because they were afraid of the Jews.” The Jews had already decided that anyone who confessed Jesus as the Christ would be put out of the synagogue. It's a pressure moment, and I think anybody who's felt that knot in their stomach understands.

Yes, baker. John 9:22 says the Jews “…had already determined that anyone who confessed Jesus as the Christ would be put out of the synagogue.” Verse 23 says that was why his parents said, “He is old enough. Ask him.” That's the pressure they were under.
That's right, friend. He says, “I already told you, and you did not listen. Why do you want to hear it again?” Then he asks if they also want to become Jesus' disciples.
That's right, baker. They say, “You are His disciple; we are disciples of Moses.” Then they add, “We know that God spoke to Moses…” They put themselves on one side and the man on the other.
Abraham is a good guess, but he isn't who they name. They say, “You are His disciple; we are disciples of Moses.” They add that they know God spoke to Moses. That's the name they claim.
Elijah is a good guess, but they don't mention him here. The Jews say, “You are His disciple; we are disciples of Moses.” They add that they know God spoke to Moses. That's the name they hold up.

The man says the very opposite, baker. He tells them, “Never before has anyone heard of opening the eyes of a man born blind.” In his words, nobody has heard of it. I think that's why it's such a big deal.
Egypt doesn't show up in his sentence, baker. He says, “If this man were not from God, He could do no such thing.” His point is about where this power comes from.
Babylon doesn't show up here, baker. The man says, “If this man were not from God, He could do no such thing.” The word he lands on is God.
The text doesn't say they go find Jesus, friend. It says they threw the man out. In verse 35, Jesus is the one who finds the man.
He doesn't ask for a sign. He says, “Who is He, Sir? Tell me so that I may believe in Him.” What he asks for is to be told who He is.
True, baker. He says, “Lord, I believe…” and he worshiped Jesus. He's the man who used to sit and beg, and now he worships Jesus. What a turn.
The text says it plainly, friend. He says, “Lord, I believe…” and he worshiped Jesus. He answers, and then he worships.

That's the question, baker. Some of the Pharisees with Him ask, “Are we blind too?” They ask it right after He says that those who see may become blind. I think it's the kind of question people ask when a statement hits close to home.
That line about where someone is from comes earlier, when the Jews talk to the man. Here the Pharisees ask Jesus, “Are we blind too?” They ask it after what He said about the blind and those who see.

That's it, baker. Jesus says, “If you were blind, you would not be guilty of sin. But since you claim you can see, your guilt remains.” He ties their guilt to their claim to see. It's a serious line, and Jesus leaves it there.
